meta.description: Genuine Wittgenstein — Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus 5.6, in C. K. Ogden's 1922 English translation. Not the corrupted "limits of my mind" paraphrase.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The limits of my language mean the limits of my world'?
meta.ogDescription: Real Wittgenstein: Tractatus 5.6, Ogden's 1922 translation of the 1921 German. Beware the popular "limits of my mind / all I have words for" misquote.

answer.label: Written by
answer.sourceLine: This is a genuine Wittgenstein line — proposition 5.6 of the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus. The German (“Die Grenzen meiner Sprache bedeuten die Grenzen meiner Welt”) first appeared in 1921; the exact English wording here is C. K. Ogden’s 1922 translation, confirmed against the full text.

source.excerpt: 5.6 The limits of my language mean the limits of my world. … 5.62 … that the world is my world, shows itself in the fact that the limits of the language (the language which only I understand) mean the limits of my world.
trail: Confirmed word-for-word against proposition 5.6 in the full text of Ogden’s translation at Wikisource.
Listed in the sourced section of Wikiquote under Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (1922), with the German original given.
Attributed to Tractatus 5.6 (1921) by the quotation archive WIST.
source.excerptNote: As rendered in C. K. Ogden’s 1922 English translation of the Tractatus, propositions 5.6 and 5.62.
source.rightsNote: The German original was published in 1921 and C. K. Ogden’s English translation — the source of this exact wording — appeared in 1922. Both predate 1931, so the text is in the public domain in the United States.

author.name: Ludwig Wittgenstein
author.heading: About Ludwig Wittgenstein
author.bio: Ludwig Wittgenstein (1889–1951) was an Austrian-born philosopher who did much of his work at Cambridge and is regarded as one of the most important thinkers of the 20th century. His early masterwork, the Tractatus Logico-Philosophicus (German 1921, English 1922), argued that the structure of language mirrors the structure of the world — and that what cannot be said clearly must be passed over in silence. Proposition 5.6 is among its most quoted lines.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: The attribution to Wittgenstein is correct — but a corrupted version of the line circulates just as widely, and it changes the meaning.

items.scope: the popular “limits of my mind” variant
items.why: A much-shared version reads “The limits of my language are the limits of my mind. All I know is what I have words for.” Wittgenstein wrote “world,” not “mind,” and the second sentence appears nowhere in the Tractatus. Wikiquote records it only as a variant translation of 5.6 (not in its Misattributed or Disputed sections); we flag it as corrupted because the “mind” wording changes the meaning.

Because the line is translated from German, wording varies by edition — you’ll see “mark the limits” or “stand for the limits” alongside “mean.” The German verb is bedeuten; the “mean” wording is Ogden’s 1922 rendering, also used by later translators.

misattribution.truthLine: The genuine line is “The limits of my language mean the limits of my world” — Tractatus 5.6, verifiable in Ogden’s translation.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: In the Tractatus, 5.6 is not a slogan about vocabulary size but a claim about logic: for Wittgenstein, the limits of language and the limits of thought about the world are one and the same, because a meaningful proposition is a picture of a possible state of affairs. What you cannot frame in language, you cannot frame as a fact of your world.
The line reads as inspirational on a poster, but its home is a dense, numbered treatise whose final proposition is “Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.”
